pageTitle: Elephants Pick Up Good Vibrations -- Through Their Feet
quote: It turns out that foot stomping and low-frequency rumbling also generate seismic waves in the ground that can travel nearly 20 miles along the surface of the Earth, according to a new study in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (JASA). More astonishing is the discovery that elephants may be able to sense these vibrations through their feet ... "Seismic waves could travel from their toenails to the ear via bone conduction, or through somatosensory receptors in the foot similar to ones found in the trunk. We think it may be a combination of both." ... "Based on our mathematical models, we estimate that seismic signals produced by elephants can travel between 10 and 20 miles in the ground"
unsupported: "with specialized receptors in their feet and trunk" (the release says elephants may sense vibrations through the feet, via bone conduction or foot receptors similar to those in the trunk) and "They can 'hear' messages from other elephants up to 20 miles away" (20 miles is a modeled travel distance for the signal, not a shown detection range)
correctedFact: Elephants' foot stomps and low rumbles send seismic waves through the ground. Stanford researchers estimated these waves can travel 10 to 20 miles, and they think elephants sense them through their feet, either by bone conduction or with touch receptors like those in the trunk.
note: The original Stanford news page (news.stanford.edu/pr/01/elephants37.html) returned 403; ScienceDaily carries the Stanford release verbatim with Stanford as the source.

pageTitle: How This Beetle Creates 500 Explosions Per Second In Its Bum
quote: The liquid can reach up to 22 miles per hour, at temperatures of around 100 degrees Celsius. ... The beetle mixes its chemical weapons within glands in its abdomen, each of which consist of two chambers. The reservoir chamber contains a solution of hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones ... The enzymes react with the incoming chemicals in a violently explosive reaction ... The spray isn’t continuous. Instead, the beetle fires between 368 and 735 pulses every second.
unsupported: "with a rapid-fire popping sound" (not on the page); "up to 500 pulses per second" understates the page's 368 to 735 pulses per second
correctedFact: Bombardier beetles store hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones in their abdomen and mix them with enzymes to set off an explosive reaction. The spray shoots out at around 100 degrees C in rapid pulses, between 368 and 735 every second, burning and repelling predators.
note: Dean et al. 1990 (Science, PMID 2349480) gives about 500 pulses per second for Stenaptinus insignis but does not cover temperature or sound.

pageTitle: Mirror-Induced Behavior in the Magpie (Pica pica): Evidence of Self-Recognition
quote: When provided with a mark, magpies showed spontaneous mark-directed behavior. Our findings provide the first evidence of mirror self-recognition in a non-mammalian species. ... The birds were either marked with a brightly colored (yellow or red) or a black (sham) mark. ... Gerti and Goldie removed the mark after a few minutes on most of the trials with a color mark and a mirror
unsupported: "(a cleaner wrasse fish has since joined them)" (not in this paper) and "immediately" (the marked birds removed the mark after a few minutes, and the paper reports this for two birds, Gerti and Goldie)
correctedFact: In 2008, magpies gave the first evidence of mirror self-recognition in a non-mammal. Researchers put a yellow or red mark on throat feathers that a bird could only see in a mirror, and some magpies kept reaching for the mark until they had removed it.
note: The cleaner wrasse result is Kohda et al. 2019, PLOS Biology (PMC6366756), which cites the magpie study; it was not used as this fact's single source.

pageTitle: Bottlenose dolphins can use learned vocal labels to address each other
quote: Bottlenose dolphins develop their own unique identity signal, the signature whistle. This whistle encodes individual identity independently of voice features. The copying of signature whistles may therefore allow animals to label or address one another. Here, we show that wild bottlenose dolphins respond to hearing a copy of their own signature whistle by calling back.
note: The study is on bottlenose dolphins; the card says dolphins generally.

pageTitle: Synchronous Fireflies at Congaree
quote: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction that takes place in a part of the abdomen appropriately called the lantern. There the chemical luciferin combines with the enzyme luciferase, and along with oxygen, magnesium, and the energy producing compound ATP, produces light. ... The appearance of fireflies flashing in the evening is a welcome sign summer is near.
note: Britannica's 'How Do Fireflies Light Up?' was tried first and returned 403.

pageTitle: Selection for social signalling drives the evolution of chameleon colour change
quote: Here we show that evolutionary shifts in capacity for colour change in southern African dwarf chameleons (Bradypodion spp.) are associated with increasingly conspicuous signals used in male contests and courtship. ... We found no evidence for the crypsis hypothesis ... Instead, our results suggest that selection for conspicuous social signals drives the evolution of colour change in this system
unsupported: "depending on their mood" (the paper is about social signaling in male contests and courtship, not mood)
correctedFact: Chameleon color change evolved mainly for communication, not camouflage. A study of southern African dwarf chameleons found that species with the most dramatic color change flash the most conspicuous signals in male contests and courtship, and found no evidence that camouflage drove the trait.
note: Study covers dwarf chameleons (Bradypodion) only.

pageTitle: Restocking supply
quote: A worker bee can visit around 2,000 flowers per day. However, due to its capacity for carrying food sources with pollen basket or corbicula, which is part of the tibia on the hind legs. Bees can visit only around 50 to 100 flowers before having to return to the hive to dispose of their supply.
unsupported: "Their tireless work as pollinators helps produce about one-third of the food we eat" (not on the page)
correctedFact: A single honey bee worker can visit around 2,000 flowers in a day. Each trip is limited by what her pollen baskets can carry, so she visits only about 50 to 100 flowers before flying back to the hive to unload.
extraPoints: Pollinators help produce about one-third of the food we eat.
note: The page is a research photo contest caption on the University of Guelph research site, a light source for the 2,000 figure.

publisher: University of Texas Marine Science Institute
pageTitle: Communicating with Color
quote: One reason they change color is to camouflage themselves from predators and prey. But, they also use changes in color to communicate. ... These particular cephalopods use color signals to exchange information about mating, aggression, or danger. ... Because these muscles are controlled by the nervous system, cephalopods can change their color and pattern very quickly and in isolated areas. ... Some species control body posture, others control skin texture
unsupported: "or confuse predators" (the page says camouflage from predators and prey, not confusing them)
correctedFact: Octopuses and their relatives can change the color and pattern of their skin very quickly. Besides hiding from predators and prey, they use these changes to communicate, adding skin texture or body posture to signal mating, aggression or danger to one another.
note: Smithsonian Ocean's 'How Octopuses and Squids Change Color' was tried first and was unavailable (site down, 403). The UTMSI article covers cephalopods as a group, octopuses included.

pageTitle: More than stridulation: signal interaction and constraint in the complex vibroacoustic courtship of a cricket
quote: Using Acheta domesticus as a model, we conduct the first comprehensive analysis of the entirety of vibroacoustic courtship signals in crickets, including their interaction. Employing audio recording, laser vibrometry, and videorecording, we unveil a complex signal involving simultaneous wing stridulation, body tremulation, and leg drumming against the substrate in a prolonged display, unique among insects. ... Further research should delve deeper into the function of this intricate signal.
unsupported: "showcasing their fitness and charm" (the paper says the display's function still needs study) and the generalization to male crickets as a whole (the study is on the house cricket)
correctedFact: Male house crickets court with more than a song. While rubbing their wings to sing, they shake their bodies and drum their legs on the ground in a long, coordinated display that researchers describe as unique among insects.
note: Abstract read via Crossref; the Springer page blocked automated access.

pageTitle: Alex the African Grey parrot
quote: Dr. Pepperberg’s pioneering research resulted in Alex learning elements of English speech to identify 50 different objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes, quantities up to and including 6 and a zero-like concept. He used phrases such as “I want X” and “Wanna go Y”, where X and Y were appropriate object and location labels. ... Alex combined his labels to identify, request, refuse, and categorize more than 100 different items
unsupported: "mimicking human speech with astonishing accuracy", "social skills" and "displaying personalities that can change depending on their environments" (none on the page)
correctedFact: Alex, an African grey parrot studied by Irene Pepperberg, learned English labels for 50 objects, seven colors and five shapes. He used them in phrases such as "I want X" and "Wanna go Y", combining labels to identify, request, refuse and categorize more than 100 items.
extraPoints: African greys show personalities that change with their environment.
note: Evidence is from one bird, Alex. The title 'Multiple Personality Parrots' rests on the unsupported personality claim.

pageTitle: Behold The Mighty, Microscopic Water Bear
quote: Microscopic water bears, also known as tardigrades, can withstand boiling, freezing, radiation, the vacuum of space and years of dehydration. Biologist Bob Goldstein of the University of North Carolina describes the creatures and why he studies them.
unsupported: "all while going into a state of cryptobiosis" (not on the page)
correctedFact: Tardigrades, the microscopic animals also called water bears, are famously hard to kill. University of North Carolina biologist Bob Goldstein notes they can withstand boiling, freezing, radiation, the vacuum of space and years of dehydration.
note: A 2009 interview summary, not a primary paper. A peer-reviewed source would be stronger for the boiling claim in particular.

publisher: National Park Service (Glacier Bay National Park & Preserve)
pageTitle: Humpback Whale Fact Sheet
quote: Mature males sing long songs (~15 minutes) in their tropical breeding grounds as a display related to mating. In quiet acoustic conditions, humpback song can be heard approximately 50 miles away from the singer.
unsupported: "can last for 20 minutes" (the page says about 15 minutes) and "or simply to communicate with their fellow swimmers"
correctedFact: Male humpback whales sing long songs, about 15 minutes each, on their tropical breeding grounds as a display related to mating. In quiet conditions, a humpback's song can be heard roughly 50 miles from the singer.
note: NOAA Fisheries' humpback species page was tried first and has no song details.

pageTitle: Chameleon | San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants
quote: The chameleon's changing skin color plays an important role in communication among individuals. It changes under the influence of the lizard's mood, such as fear or anger, the amount of light, and the temperature or humidity. Males that can make themselves brighter are more dominant and attract more females. A submissive male displays brown or gray.
unsupported: "it's not just for camouflage" and "masters of both disguise" (the page does not mention camouflage)
correctedFact: A chameleon's color shifts with its mood, such as fear or anger, and with light, temperature and humidity. Color also carries social messages: brighter males are more dominant and attract more females, while a submissive male turns brown or gray.

pageTitle: WEC218/UW259: The Cuban Treefrog in Florida
quote: Reproduction is largely stimulated by rainfall, especially warm summer rains such as those associated with tropical weather systems and thunderstorms. ... Like most frogs, male Cuban treefrogs call to attract mates. When Cuban treefrogs are concentrated in an area for breeding, their calls may be annoying, especially following heavy rains.
unsupported: The whole core: "dubbed the 'rainmaker' because its croaking sounds can stimulate rainfall" and "can be heard from miles away". The source shows the reverse: rain stimulates breeding and calling.
note: First page tried (UF/IFAS Panhandle extension post) redirected to a listing page. Searched for a rainmaker nickname or rain-triggering calls and found none. Card needs a rewrite or removal.

publisher: SWOT Report (State of the World's Sea Turtles)
pageTitle: How Long Can Sea Turtles Hold Their Breath?
quote: The studies have found that under most conditions, sea turtles will dive for 20 to 40 minutes while foraging and up to several hours when sleeping. Additionally, when the water gets cold, some turtles are able to remain underwater for much longer.
unsupported: "up to 5 hours" (the source says several hours, for sea turtles generally), "dive deep" and "one of the ocean's most efficient swimmers"
correctedFact: Sea turtles, green turtles included, are champion breath holders. Under most conditions they dive for 20 to 40 minutes while foraging, but they can stay under for up to several hours while sleeping, and even longer in cold water.
note: NOAA Fisheries' green turtle page was tried first and gives no breath-hold figure. Article by Sarah Milton.

pageTitle: The coevolution of fungus-ant agriculture
quote: Fungus-farming ants cultivate multiple lineages of fungi for food ... We found that fungus-ant agriculture originated ~66 million years ago when the end-of-Cretaceous asteroid impact temporarily interrupted photosynthesis ... Subsequently, ~27 million years ago, one ancestral fungal cultivar population became domesticated, i.e., obligately mutualistic
unsupported: "They cut leaves" (leafcutters are not named in the abstract) and "thousands of years before humans" (the source dates ant agriculture to about 66 million years ago)
correctedFact: Fungus-farming ants grow fungi as food, and a 2024 study led by Smithsonian scientists dated the start of this ant agriculture to about 66 million years ago, right after the asteroid impact that ended the Cretaceous. Around 27 million years ago, one crop fungus became fully dependent on its ant farmers.
note: The Smithsonian press release on this study was tried first and blocked automated access (403). "Thousands of years" on the card understates the gap by a factor of thousands.

pageTitle: Sloths May Be Slow, But They're Not Stupid
quote: For instance, sloths are actually three times faster in water than they are on land, says Becky Cliffe, a zoologist and founder of the Costa Rica-based Sloth Conservation Foundation. What’s more, they float.
unsupported: "three-toed" (the page says sloths generally) and "pulling themselves along with their long front arms"
correctedFact: Sloths may be slow in the trees, but they are three times faster in water than on land, according to zoologist Becky Cliffe of the Sloth Conservation Foundation. They also float, because so much of their body weight is gassy, fermenting leaves in the gut.
note: The three-times figure is an expert's statement, not a cited measurement.

unsupported: The whole claim that common house spiders "sing" with low-frequency vibrations to attract mates
note: Searched Parasteatoda tepidariorum courtship vibration and stridulation; found only related species (Steatoda grossa, black widows, Argiope). The second page checked (Frontiers in Zoology 2014) covers black widows, not house spiders.

pageTitle: Molecular machineries of ciliogenesis, cell survival, and vasculogenesis are differentially expressed during regeneration in explants of the demosponge Halichondria panicea
quote: Sponges are interesting animal models for regeneration studies, since even from dissociated cells, they are able to regenerate completely. In particular, explants are model systems that can be applied to many sponge species, since small fragments of sponges can regenerate all elements of the adult, including the oscula and the ability to pump water. ... The ability to regenerate a lost body part is relatively common across the animal tree of life, but whole-body regeneration (WBR) is less frequent
note: Same paper notes whole-body regeneration in sponges is most likely seen in experimental conditions. Australian Museum sponge page was tried first and returned 404.

pageTitle: Cephalopod Ink: Production, Chemistry, Functions and Applications
quote: Most obvious are the mechanisms operating in the visual channel of predators. In this way, ink clouds could serve as smoke-screens behind which inking cephalopods can hide or jet escape. Pseudomorphs might mimic the form of the inking cephalopod and, by attracting the attention of the predator, buy the cephalopod time to escape ... Observational studies in the field and laboratory amply support the idea that ink defends cephalopods from predators. ... ink has been proposed as an aversive deterrent or as a disruptor of predators’ chemical senses
unsupported: "can also temporarily impair a predator's sense of smell" (the review lists this only as a proposed function, not a shown one)
correctedFact: When threatened, octopuses and other cephalopods can squirt ink. A diffuse ink cloud works as a smoke screen to hide behind or jet away from, and a mucus-rich blob called a pseudomorph can mimic the animal's shape to hold a predator's attention while it escapes.

pageTitle: Male-specific use of the purr in the ring-tailed lemur (Lemur catta)
quote: In mammals, purring has been described in mostly affiliative contexts. In the ring-tailed lemur (Lemur catta), both males and females purr, but only males were observed purring in agonistic contexts. ... My results indicate that the male ring-tailed lemur purr is used most frequently as an agonistic vocalization in male-male encounters, in addition to being used less frequently in other social contexts, including during tail-waving at females, resting, scent-marking, feeding and copulation.
unsupported: "just like cats", "primarily to communicate with their family members" and "helps strengthen social bonds and keep everyone feeling safe" (for males the study finds the purr is used most in aggressive encounters)
correctedFact: Ring-tailed lemurs purr, and both males and females do it. A field study in Madagascar found that males purr most often during tense encounters with other males, and dominant males purr more in every setting, from resting and feeding to scent-marking.
note: The source partly contradicts the card's bonding angle for males. Card says lemurs generally; the source is ring-tailed lemurs.

pageTitle: Alex the African Grey parrot
quote: Dr. Pepperberg’s pioneering research resulted in Alex learning elements of English speech to identify 50 different objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes, quantities up to and including 6 and a zero-like concept.
note: Evidence centers on one parrot, Alex. Same page as fact 85.

publisher: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia
pageTitle: Wood Frog (Rana [Lithobates] sylvatica)
quote: Breeds in fishless temporary wetlands and vernal pools. ... An explosive breeder, often beginning reproduction in late winter or early spring, sometimes before ice melts. ... Call: A short, duck-like “quack.”
unsupported: "cramming their entire mating season into just a week or two", "right as snowmelt fills" and "serenading females" (not on the page)
correctedFact: Wood frogs are explosive breeders. They often start in late winter or early spring, sometimes before the ice melts, laying eggs in fishless temporary wetlands and vernal pools. Instead of a typical frog croak, males give a short, duck-like quack.

pageTitle: Clown Anemonefish
quote: Each fish forms a relationship with a specific sea anemone, acclimating its protective mucous to the anemone’s stinging tentacles. ... Anemones provide protection for these fish as well as their nests. In return the anemone may benefit from fish consumption of parasites and increased water circulation from the fanning action of the fish’s fins. ... The anemonefish will eat the dead tentacles of the anemone and any uneaten prey that is captured by the stinging tentacles of the anemone.
unsupported: "providing each other with protection and food" (the fish gets protection and food; the anemone's stated benefits are parasite removal and water circulation)
correctedFact: Clown anemonefish live among a sea anemone's stinging tentacles, protected by a mucus coat they acclimate to their host. The anemone shelters the fish and its nest and supplies leftover prey, and in return the fish may eat the anemone's parasites and fan water through it.

pageTitle: Mayflies (Order: Ephemeroptera)
quote: Mayflies are very shortlived as adults. Most only live between one and four days. ... No food is taken ... The nymphs live in the water ... Some are able to produce up to 3 generations a year, whilst others may take up to 3 years to mature
unsupported: "sometimes living just a few hours as adults" and "mating, and then dying in the same day" (the page gives one to four days for most adults)
correctedFact: Mayflies spend most of their lives underwater as nymphs, and some species take up to three years to mature. The winged adults that finally emerge do not eat and usually live only one to four days, just long enough to swarm, mate and lay eggs.
note: A society fact file, not a university page. Title 'Butterfly Birthdays' does not match a mayfly.
